mh17: Flight MH17 is shot down over eastern Ukraine by a Buk missile. All 298 people on board are killed.
A Buk launcher brought in from Russia fires from a farm field near Pervomaiskyi and leaves the next day.
Photos and videos of the launcher appear on social media, including on Twitter and YouTube.
Bellingcat geolocates the images and follows the launcher back to Russia’s 53rd anti-aircraft brigade.
Ukraine’s security service hands over intercepted calls; telecom data places phones along the route.
The US says within days that it detected the launch, but never releases its satellite data.
The Hague court convicts three men of murder in absentia in 2022. In 2025 ICAO holds Russia responsible.
The layers that solved MH17 now run denser and mostly through US firms.
protest: A Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University co-writes an op-ed in the student newspaper.
Canary Mission, an anonymous website that profiles pro-Palestinian students, publishes a page about her.
“Catch and Revoke” uses AI to scan foreign students’ social media. Whether it flagged her is not public.
The Secretary of State revokes her student visa without telling her.
Plainclothes agents in masks detain her on a street in Somerville, Massachusetts.
ICE’s case management runs on Palantir. Its role in her case is not public.
Within a day she is moved through Vermont to a detention centre in Basile, Louisiana, far from her lawyers.
After six weeks in detention, a federal judge in Vermont orders her release. Her case continues.
border: A proposed CBP rule would make visa-waiver travellers list five years of social-media accounts for ESTA.
The Marechaussee checked air passengers’ data in a system built on Palantir software, under a 2014 contract.
Visa-waiver countries must let US officers query their police databases, or lose visa-free travel.
A DHS rule lets CBP photograph every non-citizen entering or leaving the US and match each face.
Fingerprints and faces collected across DHS are moving into HART, on Amazon Web Services’ government cloud.
Border officers can search phones without a warrant. A French scientist was refused entry in Houston.
He is put on a plane back to Europe. The decision rests on an officer’s reading of a phone.
icc: An executive order authorises sanctions on the court and designates its chief prosecutor, Karim Khan.
Sanctions bar US people and companies from providing services to those designated.
Microsoft disables the chief prosecutor’s email, the AP reports. Microsoft says it never suspended services.
The court’s own work runs on Microsoft. With its prosecutor cut off, his email moves to Proton.
US payment networks and platforms close the accounts of sanctioned officials.
Judge Nicolas Guillou loses his cards and his Amazon, Airbnb and PayPal accounts.
Under oath, Microsoft France says it cannot guarantee French data would not be handed to US authorities.
The ICC plans to replace Microsoft Office with openDesk, an open-source suite from Germany.
kenya: A trader in Nairobi turns shillings into USDT through M-Pesa and an exchange.
Tether, registered in El Salvador, issues one USDT for every dollar it receives.
Cantor Fitzgerald in New York holds most of Tether’s reserves and earns tens of millions a year in fees.
The reserves are mostly short-term US government debt: more than $141bn of exposure at the end of 2025.
Stablecoin demand pushes bill yields down. Savers abroad lend to the US government through a token.
The holder earns no interest. Kenya’s own 91-day Treasury bills paid 7.9% in September 2025.
Tether made more than $10bn of profit in 2025 and owns a portfolio of more than $20bn.
Cantor’s chief executive, Howard Lutnick, became US Commerce Secretary in 2025, pledging to divest.
Tether can freeze any USDT address. A Kenyan saver holds dollars that one company can switch off.
nexperia: The Netherlands has required export licences for ASML’s advanced chip machines to China since 2023.
The US put Wingtech, Nexperia’s Chinese owner, on its entity list. Nexperia itself was not listed.
US officials: Nexperia’s Chinese chief executive would have to be replaced, or it could lose the US market.
Washington extended its export controls to every company at least 50% owned by a blacklisted firm.
The economy ministry invoked a 1952 law; the Enterprise Chamber suspended the chief executive.
China banned exports from Nexperia’s Chinese unit, which makes about 70% of the company’s output.
European carmakers and suppliers, Volkswagen and ZF among them, warned of shortages of basic chips.
After Trump and Xi met in Busan, Washington suspended the 50% rule and Beijing granted export exemptions.
huawei: The US put Huawei on its entity list: no US technology without a licence.
Google suspended Huawei’s licence for Google Mobile Services. New models lost the Play Store, Gmail and Maps.
Outside China, new Huawei phones shipped without Google’s apps, and buyers abroad turned away.
Washington extended its rules to foreign-made chips. TSMC stopped shipping to Huawei from 15 September 2020.
Huawei could no longer have its own chip designs made. It fell from the largest smartphone seller to sixth.
Huawei sold its budget phone brand Honor.
The Mate 60 launched with a 7-nanometre chip made by China’s SMIC, running Huawei’s own HarmonyOS.
russia: The US, EU and allies froze roughly half of the Bank of Russia’s reserves of more than $600bn.
Seven Russian banks were removed from SWIFT, the messaging network banks use for cross-border payments.
Visa and Mastercard suspended operations in Russia. Cards issued in Russia stopped working abroad.
Apple and Microsoft halted sales; Oracle and SAP suspended operations.
Russia fell back on its own card scheme, Mir, its SPFS messaging system and trade settled in yuan.
The EU made the freeze open-ended: €210bn of Russian state assets, €185bn of them at Euroclear.
Profits on the frozen assets back a $50bn G7 loan to Ukraine. A plan to lend the assets themselves failed.
nayara: The EU added Nayara Energy, an Indian refiner 49.13% owned by Rosneft, to its Russia sanctions list.
Microsoft applied the EU listing to a customer in India, which does not recognise the EU sanctions.
Microsoft suspended Nayara’s Outlook, Teams and Office accounts and its access to data on its servers.
Nayara sued in the Delhi High Court. Microsoft restored the services before the next hearing.
SAP India suspended support for Nayara’s enterprise software, citing the same sanctions.
The Delhi High Court ordered SAP to restore service, ruling that Indian law governs the contract.
maven: Satellite and drone imagery of militia and weapons sites in Iraq and Syria feeds the targeting system.
Maven, the targeting system Palantir builds for the Pentagon, narrows down targets for more than 85 strikes.
Officers at Central Command approve the targets. The AI “isn’t ready to recommend the order of attack”.
US aircraft strike seven facilities in Iraq and Syria, days after a drone attack killed three US soldiers.
The Maven contract was worth $480m in May 2024; in May 2025 its ceiling was raised to about $1.3bn.
The Pentagon makes Maven a programme of record: a standing budget line paid to a private firm.
NATO buys the Maven Smart System for its own command. Allied targeting now runs on the same US software.
ice: Ordinary apps, such as weather and navigation apps, share their users’ location with advertising partners.
Gravy Analytics and its subsidiary Venntel aggregate the location data and sell it on.
ICE and CBP bought access to Venntel’s location data. ICE used it to identify immigrants later arrested.
ICE pays Palantir $30m to build ImmigrationOS, a system to select and track people for deportation.
ICE arrests and deports. Every link in the chain before the arrest was commercial.
gaza: Project Nimbus, a $1.2bn contract, gives the Israeli government cloud services from Google and Amazon.
Israel’s signals-intelligence unit records Palestinians’ phone calls at mass scale.
The recordings are stored on Azure servers in the Netherlands and Ireland.
An AI system, Lavender, marks as many as 37,000 Palestinians as suspected militants.
Officers approve strikes; sources say reviews of Lavender’s picks were often brief.
Microsoft blocks some Israeli defence-ministry accounts from the services used for the surveillance.
garantex: The Treasury sanctions Garantex, a Moscow crypto exchange. The EU follows in February 2025.
Tether freezes about $27m of USDT held in Garantex wallets, working with US authorities.
Garantex suspends all services, including withdrawals.
The US Secret Service seizes the exchange’s web domains.

cap: US commercial satellites image Russian positions; much of the imagery reaches Ukraine through US contracts.
Palantir merges satellite, drone and open-source feeds and proposes targets.
Starlink keeps commanders, spotters and drone teams connected. From June 2023 the Pentagon pays.
A drone team receives the target over Starlink and streams video back.
The target is hit, the result is checked, and the loop starts again.
Musk declines to extend Starlink coverage for a drone attack on the Russian fleet near Crimea.
Washington pauses intelligence sharing and cuts Maxar imagery for six days, until Ukraine accepts a ceasefire proposal.
SpaceX and Kyiv switch on a whitelist of verified terminals. Smuggled Russian Starlinks lose their links.

close.title: Two holders, three switches
close.text: It has three switches. SpaceX, a private company, holds two of them; Washington holds the third.
